planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this Turkish and Greek native tolerates dry to consistently moist conditions and is one of very few Old World bluestars grown alongside the North American species already in this dataset.

directions: Native to woodland margins and scrub in Turkey and Greece, this species is classified as Critically Endangered in the wild due to habitat loss and over-collection, though it remains easy and adaptable in cultivation. Narrow, lance-shaped leaves cover a woody-based, clump-forming plant topped in mid-spring with clusters of light-to-dark blue, star-shaped flowers similar in form to the American bluestars but on a more compact frame. Unlike the sun-loving Amsonia hubrichtii and A. tabernaemontana already in this dataset, this species tolerates a wider range of light from full sun into partial shade. Foliage turns a clear yellow in fall and the plant is essentially pest-free and drought tolerant once established.

common_name: Halfway to Arkansas Bluestar (Dwarf Fringed Amsonia)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this compact selection stays about half the size of full-sized threadleaf bluestars, so it fits smaller borders and front-of-bed plantings where the larger species would overwhelm the space.

directions: Introduced by plant breeder Brent Horvath of Intrinsic Perennial Gardens in Hebron, Illinois, this hybrid selection traces its fine, needle-like foliage to Amsonia ciliata parentage but forms a noticeably smaller, denser, more rounded mound than the popular Amsonia hubrichtii cultivars already in this dataset. Sky-blue, star-shaped flowers open in late spring above the deep green, thread-fine foliage, which moves visibly in the slightest breeze, an effect sometimes described as a 'motion' plant. Like its relatives, it colors a rich gold in autumn, tolerates heat and drought once established, and is rarely bothered by deer or rabbits.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this award-winning cultivar forms a tight basal mound well suited to shaded border edges and mixed shade containers.

directions: Bred from a controlled cross between a proprietary Heuchera seed parent and a cut-leaf Tiarella pollen parent, this cultivar carries palmately lobed, blue-green foliage marked by a bold, dark central pattern that follows the leaf veins and is overlaid with a silvery sheen through spring and summer, fading toward plain green in fall and winter. Numerous slender stalks of warm pink flowers rise above the foliage mound in late spring, and the plant has earned recognition from the Royal Horticultural Society for its combined foliage and flower display. It stays compact and mounded rather than spreading aggressively, making it a tidy choice for shaded edging.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial sun to shade; its trailing stems make it well suited to hanging baskets, raised planters, or as a spilling groundcover over a shaded slope or wall.

directions: The second release in Terra Nova Nurseries' trailing 'Falls' series alongside 'Redstone Falls' already in this dataset, this cultivar was bred specifically for a cascading rather than mounding habit. Chartreuse, lobed leaves are marked with deep crimson veining radiating from the center, and pink-and-white flowers open in spring above the foliage. Stems trail two to three feet in a container, making it useful as a hanging-basket specimen or a spreading groundcover in the shade garden, and the spring flowers draw bees and other pollinators.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this cultivar tolerates drier shade better than many heucherellas once its root system is established.

directions: Bred by Charles Oliver of The Primrose Path nursery in Pennsylvania, this cultivar forms a compact basal mound of rounded, lobed, bronze-based leaves overlaid with a metallic silver sheen and flushed red-purple on the undersides, maturing to a darker bronze-green as the season progresses. Small, white, bell-shaped flowers open in airy panicles on slender, wiry, dark stems that rise well above the foliage mound from late spring into midsummer. It earned a blue ribbon at a Dutch horticultural exhibition in 1997 and holds a US plant patent, and its tolerance of drier shade sets it apart from many moisture-loving heucherella cultivars.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; its smaller, more compact growth habit suits tighter garden spaces than older, larger-leaved brunnera cultivars.

directions: Developed through a controlled breeding program in Illinois from a proprietary compact, blue-flowered Brunnera macrophylla parent selection and later patented in the United States, this cultivar produces smaller-than-typical heart-shaped leaves densely coated in silver over a medium-green base. Its tidier, more restrained clumping habit stays noticeably more compact than many older silver-leaf brunnera selections, making it easier to fit into small shaded borders. Small sprays of clear blue, forget-me-not-like flowers rise above the emerging foliage in early spring.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; its variegated margin holds up to sun better than many silver-leaf brunneras but still colors best out of hot afternoon exposure.

directions: Discovered in 1997 in Chimacum, Washington, as a naturally occurring sport in a tissue-cultured batch of the cultivar 'Langtrees' already in this dataset, this brunnera bears wide, heart-shaped leaves edged with a thin cream-white margin and an overall silvery surface sheen, separated from the edge by a band of gray-green that gives each leaf a distinctive two-toned, wing-like pattern. Small clusters of violet-blue, forget-me-not-style flowers open in early spring above the emerging foliage clump. Its variegated margin is reported to resist summer leaf scorch better than many other silver-patterned brunnera selections.
